nameStory: The name 'Bald Spikerush' comes from its distinctive flower head that looks like a tiny spike at the tip of each stem, combined with its relatively bare or 'bald' appearance compared to other rushes. Unlike true rushes, spikerushes have their flowers clustered in a single compact spike rather than spread out in branching clusters.
description: Bald Spikerush is a small, grass-like wetland plant that forms clumps of slender, upright stems. Each thin green stem is topped with a single, oval-shaped flower spike that's about the size of a grain of rice. The plant typically grows 4-12 inches tall and has no visible leaves - just the smooth, round stems rising directly from the wet soil. It's one of the more delicate-looking members of the sedge family.

idTips.label: Flower Spikes
idTips.description: Single small oval spike at the tip of each stem, reddish-brown to tan colored, about 1/4 inch long and feels slightly papery when touched

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Thin, smooth, round stems with no leaves - roll easily between your fingers and feel firm but flexible like thin wire

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms small tufts or loose colonies in wet soil, with multiple stems arising from creeping underground parts

idTips.label: Height
idTips.description: Compact size, usually staying under one foot tall, making it one of the shorter spikerushes you'll encounter

habitat: Found in wet, alkaline soils around lake shores, pond edges, and seasonal wetlands, particularly in areas with limestone or calcium-rich soils. In New England, it's extremely rare and tends to occur in calcareous wetlands and wet prairies where the soil stays moist through most of the growing season.

seasonality.spring: New green stems begin emerging from the soil in late spring, looking like tiny green needles poking up from wet ground.
seasonality.summer: Flower spikes develop and mature, turning from green to reddish-brown, with seeds ripening by late summer.
seasonality.fall: Stems begin to turn brown and flower spikes become more papery and pale, eventually releasing tiny seeds.
seasonality.winter: Dead stems may persist through winter as brown stubble in frozen wetlands, but most growth dies back to underground parts.

funFact: Despite being called a 'rush,' Bald Spikerush is actually in the sedge family, and you can remember this with the old botanist's rhyme: 'Sedges have edges' - if you look closely at the stem cross-section, it's actually triangular, not perfectly round like true rushes!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other small spikerushes, especially Needle Spikerush, but Bald Spikerush has noticeably wider, more oval flower spikes rather than the very narrow, needle-like spikes of its relatives. The reddish coloring of the mature spikes also helps distinguish it from the typically brown spikes of Common Spikerush.
contextualKnowledge: With only one recorded observation in New England, this is one of our region's rarest plants - finding one would be like discovering botanical treasure! It's much more common in the Great Plains and western North America, making any New England sighting particularly noteworthy.
compareHints: Among the spikerushes, Bald Spikerush stands out for its particularly wide, oval flower spikes with a reddish tint, unlike the narrow spikes of Needle Spikerush or the larger, brown spikes of Common Spikerush. It's also one of the shorter species in the genus, rarely exceeding a foot in height. The reddish coloration that gives it its scientific name 'erythropoda' (meaning red-footed) is often the best field mark to separate it from look-alikes.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among the many spikerush species in New England, blunt spikerush stands out for its soft, spongy stems and distinctly rounded spikelets.
Needle Spikerush is the most delicate of all New England spikerushes, with stems so thin they make other species look chunky by comparison.
Unlike other spikerushes that grow in shallow water or wet soil, Robbins' Spikerush is the deep-water specialist of the genus, growing fully submerged in 1-4 feet of water.

Among the many spikerush species in New England, Black-fruited Spikerush is most easily distinguished by its dark seeds - Common Spikerush has pale tan seeds, while Needle Spikerush is much more delicate with thread-like stems.
Among the many New England spikerushes, Yellow Spikerush stands out for its pale, yellowish coloring and smaller stature compared to Common Spikerush or Blunt Spikerush.
Among New England spikerushes, common spikerush is distinguished by its robust, colony-forming habit and relatively large flower spikes.
Among New England's many spikerush species, Small Spikerush is distinguished by its extremely short stature (under 4 inches) and preference for salty habitats.
Among New England's many spikerushes, Matted Spikerush is unique for its low, mat-forming growth habit - all its relatives grow upright.
Among its many spikerush relatives in New England, ovate spikerush stands out with its distinctly oval or egg-shaped flower spikes - most other spikerushes have more cylindrical or pointed spikes.
Among New England's many spikerushes, Slender Spikerush stands out for its particularly thin stems and small, oval flower spikes.
Among New England's spikerushes, Wright's is distinguished by its small size and the distinctive pyramid-shaped tubercle on its seeds.
Among the many New England spikerushes, Horsetail Spikerush is unique for its hollow, jointed stems - most other spikerushes have solid stems without visible segments.
Among the many spikerush species in New England, squarestem spikerush is the only one with distinctly four-angled stems - all the others have round or slightly flattened stems.

Few-flower Spikerush stands out from its many spikerush relatives primarily by its sparse flower count - most other New England spikerushes like Common Spikerush or Blunt Spikerush have dense, crowded spikelets with dozens of flowers.
Among New England's many spikerushes, Long-tubercled Spikerush stands out for its exceptionally large tubercle - up to 2.
Beaked spikerush differs from its many spikerush relatives primarily in its habitat preferences and the distinctive beaked tubercle on its seeds.
Among New England's spikerushes, Slender Spikerush has the thinnest stems - much thinner than Common Spikerush or Blunt Spikerush.

Unlike Common Spikerush which has smooth, round stems, or Needle Spikerush which forms dense mats of hair-thin stems, Threerib Spikerush is the only species in the genus with distinctly three-ribbed stems.
Among New England's many spikerushes, Creeping Spikerush is unique for its mat-forming, spreading growth pattern via underground runners.
